purpose: Tacrolimus is used to help prevent your body from rejecting a transplanted organ, such as a kidney, liver, or heart. It is also sometimes used as a skin ointment to treat certain skin conditions like eczema. Keeping your transplanted organ working well is the main goal of this medicine.
how_it_works: Your immune system is designed to attack things it sees as foreign — including a transplanted organ. Tacrolimus works by calming down a key part of your immune system so it does not attack your new organ. Think of it like turning down the volume on your immune system just enough to protect your transplant without shutting it off completely.
common_side_effects: Common side effects include shaking or tremors in your hands, headache, high blood pressure, high blood sugar, nausea, diarrhea, trouble sleeping, and kidney problems. You may also feel more tired than usual. Let your doctor know if any of these bother you.
warnings: Because this medicine lowers your immune system, you are more likely to get infections — even serious ones — so wash your hands often and avoid sick people. Long-term use can slightly increase the risk of certain cancers, especially skin cancer, so use sunscreen and protect your skin from the sun. Never stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first, as stopping suddenly can cause your body to reject your organ. Tell all your doctors and pharmacist about every medicine, supplement, or herbal product you take, since many things can change how tacrolimus works in your body.
typical_dosing: Dosing is very personal and based on your body weight, the type of transplant you had, and your blood levels of the medicine. It is usually taken by mouth twice a day (or once a day for the extended-release forms), with or without food — but always the same way each time. Your doctor will do regular blood tests to make sure your dose is just right — not too much and not too little.
